summary: FlameSight is a dashboard that turns NASA's microgravity combustion research into fire-safety insight for spacecraft and Moon and Mars habitats. NASA's PSI repository and technical reports hold hundreds of documents that are hard to search, while planned habitats use oxygen-rich, low-pressure air (about 30% O2 at 70 kPa) where fire behaves differently. We processed 448 NASA documents and data files, including 90 spreadsheet and CSV data files from the PSI repository, into 30 investigations, 307 key findings (each with an exact quote, document and page) and 1,979 test runs copied from NASA's own data tables. Users can ask questions and get cited answers, or "Not in the data" when the sources say nothing; explore and compare investigations by oxygen, pressure and flow; see which studies come closest to a Moon-base atmosphere; and read 281 ranked safety insights. Every claim links to the NASA page it came from. The data set is a preliminary extraction (v0.1) and is labelled unverified in the app.
details:
What it does. FlameSight answers one question: what has NASA already learned about fire in space, and how close is it to the atmosphere of a Moon base? The dashboard has five parts. Ask answers plain-language questions only from NASA sources, with citations (paper and page) and an evidence badge (number of tests, platform, repeats), and says "Not in the data" when nothing relevant is found. Explore and Compare filter the 30 investigations and 1,979 test runs by fuel, oxygen, pressure, flow and hardware and compare experiments side by side. Coverage Map shows which tests match the planned Moon-base atmosphere (at least 30% O2 at no more than 70.3 kPa): only 22 of 1,979 runs do. Ranked Insights scores each finding by safety impact x evidence strength x mission relevance. Safety Margin compares the lowest oxygen level at which a material still burned in normal gravity and in microgravity.

How it works. A Python pipeline downloads NASA documents (PSI repository, NTRS, NASA web pages), extracts text and tables, and splits them into 13,928 cited passages. Test runs are copied cell by cell from 21 NASA test tables, and where NASA's own numbers exist they win over extracted ones. 307 key findings were extracted with AI assistance (Claude Code); code then checks that every finding's quote appears on its cited page (307 of 307 pass). Evidence strength and Moon-base relevance are computed by rules; safety impact is judged against a written rubric, and rankings are marked reviewed only after a team member checks them. The Q&A service combines vector search (all-MiniLM-L6-v2) with keyword search over the findings and passages, then either quotes the closest verified findings or, with a Claude API key, writes a short answer using only the retrieved sources. A FastAPI backend serves the data to a Next.js dashboard.

Benefits. Designers and safety engineers get one searchable, cited map of 30 investigations instead of hundreds of reports. Examples it surfaces: NASA's own guide states that its standard flammability test (Test 1) is not conservative; in Saffire VI, fire growth on PMMA rose 73% for 0.08 more oxygen even though pressure fell 45%; and the ISS smoke detector missed smoke from wiring insulation in some tests. It also shows the gaps: no test in our data was run at lunar gravity.

Limits (stated in the app). The data is a v0.1 extraction and has not had NASA review; only the top 33 insights have been reviewed by a team member. The Q&A test set gives 26/27 answers citing the right finding and 0/17 off-topic questions answered, but only 4/6 and 2/4 on two held-out sets. Outcomes are classified for 736 of 1,979 test runs. From the PSI repository we used its documents and its spreadsheet and CSV data tables; its raw instrument files and videos (more than 16,000 files are catalogued for these investigations) were not downloaded.

Goals. Extend the data to more investigations (for example the missing BASS-I and SPICE reports), have a combustion scientist verify the extraction, and add lunar-gravity results as they are published.

Tools and languages. Python (data pipeline, FastAPI services), TypeScript (Next.js dashboard), SQLite, ChromaDB, ONNX Runtime; full list under "Space Agency Partner Data and Other References".
